item.title: Nd isotopes as a paleocirculation tracer: consideration of sedimentary context and assessment through a north-south Atlantic transect
item.dc:creator: Joohee Kim, Maria Jaume‐Seguí, Karla P. Knudson, Maayan Yehudai, Leopoldo David Pena, Chandranath Basak, … (+2)
item.description:
Quaternary Science Reviews — matched: Atlantic meridional overturning circulation, AMOC, overturning circulation, ocean circulation, interglacial, glacial cycle, sediment core
Authigenic neodymium (Nd) isotope ratios have been extensively used over the past two decades to reconstruct past changes in the global ocean circulation. Nevertheless, their effectiveness as a water mass tracer is currently strongly disputed based on the potential for modification by non-conservative processes. This study compares authigenic Nd isotope records along a meridional transect in the Atlantic from sediment core sites chosen with careful consideration of sedimentary conditions that are conducive to preserving the original seawater signal, including high carbonate/low lithogenic detritus content, oxic conditions, and exclusion of sites near continental margins and regions impacted by local effects. Records over the last 1.5 Myr shows north-to-south patterns such that, with few exceptions, at each point in time, at nearly every location, Nd isotope ratios are lower toward the north, and higher toward the south. The same relationship is observed in seawater studies of the present-day Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) . Moreover, each site shows interglacial-glacial cyclicity, indicating systemic changes through time impacting the entire Atlantic basin. In addition, a comparison of Nd isotope records over the last glacial cycle reaffirms these same meridional trends at high temporal resolution. The coherence of the present-day circulation dynamics and past meridional Nd isotope patterns provide strong evidence that such transects can be used to track temporal changes in the water mass structure and circulation in the Atlantic, if the deep-sea cores are carefully chosen for favorable conditions to preserve the original seawater Nd isotope signature.

item.title: Hydroclimatic changes in southeastern Mongolia from the earlier Late Pleistocene to the mid-Holocene: a multi-proxy record from a glacier-decoupled closed-basin sedimentary sequence in Bayan Tohom Gobi
item.dc:creator: Sumin Kang, Altansukh Ochir, Yukiya Tanaka
item.description:
Quaternary International — matched: glacier, last glacial maximum, Holocene, proxy, radiocarbon
This study reconstructs hydroclimatic changes from the earlier Late Pleistocene to the mid-Holocene using the 3.88 m BT-1 trench profile in Bayan Tohom Gobi, southeastern Mongolia (45°06′50.6″ N, 112°31′47.1″ E; ∼970 m a.s.l.). Accelerator mass spectrometry radiocarbon and optically stimulated luminescence dating provide discrete chronological constraints for grain-size and geochemical records interpreted using end-member modelling and principal component analysis. Organic-rich fine basin fill deposited during the earlier Late Pleistocene is separated by a sharp contact, potentially representing erosion or non-deposition, from coarse sedimentation within a broadly constrained later-glacial interval encompassing the Last Glacial Maximum. This coarse deposition involved aeolian input, basin-floor reworking, and episodic runoff, followed by finer sedimentation during the deglacial interval. Shallow-water to playa deposition, with its onset broadly bracketed around the Younger Dryas–Early Holocene transition, was accompanied by HCl-soluble enrichment consistent with carbonate accumulation, before renewed fine-grained shallow-water or wetland deposition during the Early to mid-Holocene. The glacier-decoupled BT-1 archive records changes in effective moisture and sediment mobility governed by precipitation, local runoff, potential groundwater input, and temperature-dependent evaporation. Comparison with Lake Ulaan and Orog Nuur highlights the influence of catchment water and sediment sources on the expression of regional hydroclimatic change in Mongolian closed basins.

item.title: Empirical constraints on ice cliff calving
item.dc:creator: Caroline T. Needell, Catherine Colello Walker, J. N. Bassis
item.description:
Science — matched: ice sheet, calving, parameterization
When calving cliffs at the margins of Earth’s ice sheets exceed a critical height, runaway retreat may be initiated in a process called the marine ice cliff instability. However, sufficiently tall ice cliffs have rarely been observed. To address this gap, we measured the characteristics of 15,330 ice cliffs across Earth’s ice sheet margins using laser altimetry. We show that cliff height is highly correlated with mélange thickness, water depth, and crevassing. We found that tall cliffs calve more rapidly than parameterizations assume, but dynamic thinning and retreat into regions with low ice thickness gradients prevent runaway retreat. These observations suggest that model projections may underestimate subannual rates of cliff calving, but that the potential for instability will depend sensitively on additional quantities, not cliff height alone.

item.title: Cascading Cryosphere Hazards in a Warming Himalaya A Secondary-Data Analysis of the August 2026 Nepal–Tibet Glacier-Collapse Debris Flow
item.dc:creator: Vipan Kumar, Ashish Nag, HARISH KUMAR, Payal Sood, Gaurav
item.category: International Journal of Sociology and Social Research
item.description:
International Journal of Sociology and Social Research — matched: cryosphere, glacier, climate change
The glacier temporarily blocked the Lhende Khola River, then released a destructive debris flow that travelled through the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli corridors into the districts of Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading in Nepal. This paper relies on secondary data from government disaster management bureaucracies and reporting from the United Nations, multilateral banks, and print and broadcast media. It focuses on the events surrounding the disaster, analysis of causal factors, casualties, damage to infrastructure and the economy, and response efforts by the government and international agencies. On August 29, 2026, the toll in Nepal was reported to be 675 dead with 2,478 missing and over 93,000 affected, while Tibet reported 7 dead and 560 missing persons. The calamity destroyed about 430 megawatts of hydropower capacity, 19 bridges, and 40 kilometres of road, while obliterating the vital Gyirong border crossing for Nepal-China trade. This paper discusses the event in the context of available scientific literature on glacial lake outburst floods (GLOFs) and ice–rock avalanches in High Mountain Asia, highlighting that the same Bhote Koshi corridor faced a similar transboundary glacial lake outburst event in 2016, which points to an issue of recurrent and unmitigated risk. The study finds there are still gaps in cross-border early detection, information sharing across borders, and infrastructure management based on climate risks, and gives some suggestions for governance and engineering. This study provides an early and organised description of a quickly changing disaster which will be useful for investigators, practitioners in civil defence planning, and policy-makers, but it also notes the limits of this investigation using secondary sources. Keywords: glacier collapse; debris flow; glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF); Himalayan cryospheric hazards; transboundary disaster governance; hydropower vulnerability; Nepal; Tibet Autonomous Region; climate change adaptation; Uttarakhand

item.title: Interpretable Relations between Tropical Sea Surface Temperature and U.S. Precipitation in Winter Season Forecasts
item.dc:creator: Michelle L. L’Heureux, Michael K. Tippett
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: predictability, sea surface temperature, Earth system
Abstract We explore the large-scale relations between anomalies of global tropical sea surface temperature (SST) and U.S. precipitation to assess the sources of December–February (DJF) predictability and skill. Canonical Correlation Analysis (CCA) is applied to forecasts from NOAA’s latest seasonal prediction system, the Seamless System for Prediction and EArth System Research (SPEAR). We find that DJF skill can largely be recreated using two SST principal components (PCs) and four precipitation PCs. However, the leading CCA modes based on these PCs are a blend of two climate signals, El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and linear trends, which makes them difficult to interpret. We separate the trend and ENSO signals using partial CCA whereby CCA is applied twice: once to data with linear trends removed and once to data with the Niño-3.4 index linearly removed. When both signals are removed, CCA finds no consequential relations. Therefore, ENSO and linear trends alone explain the predictable parts of the winter forecast of tropical SST and U.S. precipitation anomalies. Despite SPEAR model predictions representing both linear and non-linear variability, skill is mostly explained by these simpler linear CCA patterns.

item.title: Persistent regional asymmetry with apparent late-record convergence in Eurasian-North American snowmelt trends
item.dc:creator: Caleb G. Pan, Sydney Baratta, Jorge Gonzalez, Sean Griffin, Kristofer Lasko, Jeremy Johnston, … (+3)
item.description:
Environmental Research Communications — matched: boreal forest, reanalysis
Abstract Northern Hemisphere snowmelt phenology has shifted earlier over the past 37 years, but Eurasia and North America have followed markedly different trajectories. Using a random forest framework fusing passive microwave brightness temperatures, ERA5-Land reanalysis, and static landscape predictors, we produce annual 6.25 km outputs of main melt onset date (MMOD), snow off date, and snowmelt duration (SMD) across the Northern Hemisphere seasonal snow domain from 1988-2025, trained on more than 13,000 in situ observations. Over the full record, median MMOD and snow off trends are roughly four to five times stronger in Eurasia (~-2 days decade⁻¹) than in North America (~-0.4 days decade⁻¹), while SMD shows little systematic change in either continent, indicating that the dominant signal is a shift in timing rather than melt-season length. A 15-year moving-window analysis shows that this full-period contrast obscures a converging trajectory: Eurasia developed a robust earlier-melt regime by the early 2000s, while North America's trends were weak or even reversed in early decades before becoming more negative in recent windows. Disaggregating by snow regime reveals that this apparent hemispheric convergence is largely an artifact of buffering within area-dominant boreal forest and tundra regimes, where trends weaken or stabilize over time, while smaller seasonal snow regimes, including prairie, montane forest, and ephemeral snow, exhibit stronger, often asymmetric, accelerations toward earlier melt, with the most coherent advances concentrated in Eurasia. These results indicate that hemispheric-scale convergence in snowmelt timing masks substantial, regime-dependent asymmetry, with direct implications for runoff timing and water availability in climatically sensitive seasonal snow environments.

item.title: Shortened Wet Seasons in the Southern Hemisphere Land under Global Warming
item.dc:creator: Jinyuan Guo, Fengfei Song, Lu Dong, Tianjun Zhou, Jian Lu, Lai-Yung Ruby Leung, … (+1)
item.description:
Journal of Climate — matched: CMIP, global warming
Abstract The annual cycle of precipitation is a distinct phenomenon in most tropical and subtropical land regions. It is normally characterized by amplitude, phase, and length of wet and dry seasons. Previous studies have documented changes in amplitude and phase under global warming, but changes in wet season length are not fully understood. Here, we show that, in the Northern Hemisphere, onset and cessation shift later at a similar pace, resulting in modest changes in wet season length. In contrast, significant changes in wet season length are primarily concentrated in the Southern Hemisphere, where 23 of the 27 CMIP6 models project a shortening of the wet season, with a multi-model mean reduction of 3.70 days. This shortening is accompanied by a larger delay in wet season onset than in cessation. The shortened wet season over the Southern Hemisphere is closely aligned with asymmetric changes in the divergence of atmospheric energy transport between the onset and cessation stages based on the atmospheric energetic framework. Asymmetric changes in the divergence of atmospheric energy are mainly determined by the net energy input to the atmosphere, dominated by the latent heat flux. Future asymmetric changes in latent heat flux are strongly influenced by precipitation-latent heat flux coupling. In the current climate, this coupling is stronger during the onset stage than during the cessation stage, leading to more pronounced changes in latent heat flux during onset relative to cessation. The resulting robust shortening of wet season length could have broad implications for ecosystems and societies.
